The Best Fishing Spots and Aquatic Experiences to Enjoy Around Lexington During Breeders’ Cup Weekend

September 18, 2026 OnFolio Admin

The Breeders’ Cup is just around the corner, and this is the perfect excuse to book your next trip built around horse racing, but with so many other things to do and see.
This year, the Breeders’ Cup is returning to Keeneland on October 30 and 31, which puts visitors in Central Kentucky during a genuinely interesting period for fishing. Kentucky Fish and Wildlife also points out that fish often feed more aggressively during fall as they prepare for winter; on top of that, the cooling water can bring bass toward shallower waters.
So, if you enjoy fishing and you plan on going to the Breeders’ Cup, Kentucky is in the perfect season for catching some big fish. Here are some of the best fishing spots near Lexington.

Jacobson Park Is the Easy Pre-Racing Option

For people who want to fish without turning the outing into a separate road trip, the best starting spot is Jacobson Park.
The park sits in Lexington itself, so it is very close, and contains a 46.3-acre lake with bank access, a fishing pier, and limited boating. Keep in mind that gas motors are not allowed, which keeps things calmer and more relaxing.
But the important thing is that for Breeders’ Cup visitors, the timing is quite good. Why? Well, if we see Kentucky Fish and Wildlife’s records, we can see that 3,000 rainbow trout were stocked into Jacobson Park Lake on October 21. This is very close to the Breeders’ Cup Championship.
So, the odds of catching fish are probably higher than picking the winner on the race itself. Even as a beginner. But if you want both to catch fish and pick the winner of the race, you should learn more about betting strategies covered in this Breeders’ Cup betting guide.
That makes Jacobson ideal for a relaxed two- or three-hour session rather than an expedition requiring coolers, satellite navigation, and a discussion about whose boat trailer is making that noise.

Elkhorn Creek Is the Place for Smallmouth Bass

If you want something wilder, head toward Elkhorn Creek.
Kentucky Fish and Wildlife describes the main stem east of Frankfort as one of Central Kentucky’s best-known streams for fishing and floating. Smallmouth bass are the major attraction, alongside rock bass and channel catfish. From the Forks of Elkhorn down toward the Kentucky River, the department identifies roughly 13 miles of paddling and fishing opportunities with several public-access points.
This is a much more active experience than sitting beside a park lake.
You can wade suitable sections or turn the day into a canoe or kayak float. Kentucky Fish and Wildlife maintains several Voluntary Public Access locations, plus put-in and take-out points along the creek. One state guide describes the stretch around Knight’s Bridge and Peaks Mill as particularly consistent for smallmouth bass.
The important thing is to check water levels before going. Streams change quickly after rainfall, and the department publishes recommended levels specifically for boating and fishing on Elkhorn.

The Kentucky River Palisades Give You the Best Scenery

For pure scenery, the Kentucky River south of Lexington may be the winner.
Pools 8 and 9 run through sections of the Kentucky River Palisades, where the river cuts between tall limestone cliffs. Kentucky Fish and Wildlife calls Pool 8, just southeast of Nicholasville, one of the most scenic and productive pools in the area, with largemouth, smallmouth, and spotted bass in tributary creeks and occasional muskellunge.
Pool 9 offers an especially attractive half-day paddle. The department describes a roughly six-mile route beginning at Fort Boonesborough State Park and ending at Clays Ferry, with opportunities for black bass, crappie, bluegill, and muskie along the way.
This is a good choice if fishing is only half the objective.

Herrington Lake Is Better for a Proper Lake Day

If you have most of Thursday available, Herrington Lake gives you a larger-water experience without travelling across half the state.
Kentucky Fish and Wildlife lists Herrington as a 2,649-acre fishery with several public access sites and boat ramps. The lake supports largemouth bass along with white and hybrid striped bass, among other species.
This is more suited to someone bringing a boat, arranging one locally, or approaching the outing as a serious fishing day rather than something squeezed between breakfast and an afternoon horse-farm tour.
Late October also suits lake fishing surprisingly well. Kentucky Fish and Wildlife notes that cooling autumn conditions encourage predator fish to feed, with bass often using flats, rocky banks, points, and creek arms as forage moves during the season.

Cave Run Lake Is Worth Sacrificing a Full Day

If fishing is a genuine priority rather than simply something pleasant to do around the Breeders’ Cup, Cave Run Lake is the trip I would save a full day for.
The reservoir lies east of Lexington near Morehead within the Daniel Boone National Forest. The lake is approximately 8,270 acres, surrounded by wooded hills and extensive recreation areas.
The headline species is muskie.
Kentucky’s 2026 fishing forecast specifically identifies Cave Run among the state’s important muskellunge waters, and the department’s fall guidance notes that muskies begin moving from their deeper summer habitat toward shallower areas as temperatures cool.
Cave Run also supports bass, crappie, and other reservoir species, so you do not have to dedicate your entire day to pursuing a fish famous for making grown adults question their recreational choices.

Final Thoughts

So, you can definitely build an entire fishing trip around the Breeders’ Cup Championships. Late October is a surprisingly good season for fishing.
You get to enjoy some of the best landscapes and some high-end horse racing and have a good time. What more can you want?
